newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND OFFERS VIETNAM SHIPYARD CREDIT, UNION ANGRY.
newsitem.headline: POLAND OFFERS VIETNAM SHIPYARD CREDIT, UNION ANGRY.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity union, battling to save the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, on Wednesday denounced a Polish government offer to provide $70 million in credit to Vietnam for modernisation of its Ha Long shipyard.
Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz made the offer to his counterpart Vo Van Kiet on Tuesday at the start of a two-day visit to Warsaw by the Vietnamese premier.

"The prime minister (Cimoszewicz) expressed the readiness of the Polish side to extend to Vietnam a $70 million government credit for modernisation of Ha Long shipyard which was once built by Poles," a Polish government statement said.
Solidarity's Gdansk leadership said it had nothing against supporting countries that needed help.

"But in view of our shipbuilding industries' difficulties, including those of the Gdansk yard, Premier Cimoszewicz's initiative bears the hallmarks of economic sabotage," the union said in a statement reported by PAP news agency.

It said the proposal amounted to "supporting competitors on the world shipbuilding market at the cost to the domestic industry of a sum which could restructure our yards so that they could rival world standards."
According to the Polish government statement, Kiet offered preferential treatment of Polish exports of machinery and other equipment for use in modernising Vietnam's economy.
Vietnam is seeking Polish participation in updating such sectors as coal and copper mining, chemicals, food processing and shipbuilding, it added.

Before the 1989 fall of communism in Poland, Warsaw provided its ideological ally Vietnam with extensive grant aid and built or equipped Ha Long as well as about 20 other major projects such as a railyard and a coal mine.
But economic exchanges have since slumped.
Cimoszewicz, a former communist turned pro-market social democrat, briefed his communist guest on Poland's economic achievements since the fall of the old system.
Kiet, 74, is visiting Poland, the Czech republic, Italy and Hungary between May 20 and 28 in a bid to revitalise ties with Vietnam's Central European former partners.
His programme on Wednesday included talks with Polish parliamentary leaders, a visit to food processing plant and a meeting with business leaders.

The Gdansk shipyard has signed a contract to build three ships, each worth $27.5 million, for a German-owned firm, reawakening hopes for reviving the enterprise where Solidarity was born 17 years ago in defiance of communism.

The deal still awaits a final agreement on financing and the union bitterly condemns the government led by ex-communists for not providing government guarantees for credits to Gdansk, saying this decision was made out of political spite.

The Polish government said this week that a plan to create a shipyard holding company founded on the successful Szczecin yard but excluding Gdansk, would be ready by mid-October. -- Anthony Barker +48 22 653 9700
